newsitem.title: USA: Some Arkansas SRW wheat yields top 100 bushels.
newsitem.headline: Some Arkansas SRW wheat yields top 100 bushels.

text.p: Yields in excess of 100 bushels per acre were reported from early harvested Arkansas soft red winter wheat fields, but yields should drop to 30 to 50 bushels in later-harvested fields, grain sources said.
"The yields have been very good," said William Johnson, University of Arkansas extension agronomist.
Wheat fields planted early last fall were producing high-yielding wheat with ideal test weights, and very little disease damage, he said.
"The test weights have been phenomenal...a lot of 58 and 60 lbs," he said.
He said one field had a three-acre section that yielded 120 bushels per acre and the entire 56-acre field averaged 108 bushels.

The U.S. Agriculture Department on June 1 estimated the average Arkansas yield to average 44 bushels per acre, but Johnson expected that to be increased to near 50 bushels. In 1996, the state yield averaged 54 bushels.

As of Sunday, 10 percent of Arkansas wheat was harvested, but Johnson said it may now be near 40 percent despite rain delays in some areas Monday and Tuesday. Areas soaked by three-inch rains late Monday could lose about 0.5 lb from average test weights.
In three to four days, when fields dry and harvest moves into later planted fields, Johnson said yields should slip to average 30 to 50 bushels.
Abundant rain last fall interrupted wheat planting and reduced acreage. Fields planted before the rain had the best yields and later planted ones, the worst, he said.

Arkansas farmers planted 880,000 acres of wheat last fall and should harvest 790,000 versus 1.24 million harvested in 1996. Crop specialists said the falls rain prevented many fields from being planted.
"We've taken in about 20 loads and the quality has been excellent," said Rick Barbee, manager of Consolidated Grain and Barge's elevator in Caruthersville in southeast Missouri.
Most of the wheat shipped to Caruthersville was from northern Arkansas, but the Missouri bootheel harvest should start this weekend, Barbee said.

Southeast Missouri fields may yield less than Arkansas' because fall rains delayed planting and spring rains prevented nitrogen applications, said Gene Stevens, a University of Missouri crop production specialist at Portageville.
"I'm not expecting a bumper crop down here," he said. "I know there are a lot of uneven stands."
Missouri's Agricultural Statistics Service said that state's wheat yield should average 45 bushels versus 39 a year ago on 1.0 million harvested acres versus 1.25 million a year ago.
The state's best wheat yields were expected in the northeast, north central and east central areas of Missouri, the service said.
